title: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
description: The co-pilot who attempted to take control of a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates pros
body: The co-pilot who attempted to take control of a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying more than 170 people plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey, before passengers managed to overpower the attacker and successfully take control of the plane.Capt Smit Machchhar said he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.A crash axe is usually kept ​in the cockpit in case of emergencies.The UAE attorney general told state media that investigations were ongoing to determine the full circumstances and motives of the incident.The co-pilot who launched the attack was an Omani national, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times have named him as Hamam al-Hammami. There has been no official confirmation of this.While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.He completed a three-year distance-learning course at Buckinghamshire New University in the UK and graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, ABC News reported. A source told the news outlet Al-Hammami did not take any pilot training at the school.Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu said that after the attacker was subdued on the flight, he called out to the crew "Kill me, kill me!"The Israeli prime minister added: "So, it's clear that he was suicidal… It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane."He also said the attacker "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination".The UAE has begun investigating whether the "incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose", according to the country's state news agency.Machchhar, who was stabbed in the attack, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.The pilot, who is from India, was in "good health and recovering well", the Indian embassy in the UAE said on Thursday."I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again," Machchhar said.About two and half hours after the plane took off from Dubai International Airport it begun to plunge sharply. The plane signalled a "general emergency" code, squawk 7700, before switching to squawk 7500, a code reporting "unlawful interference", or hijacking.In an interview with the BBC, one passenger described the moment he realised that something was wrong.Almog Itali said: "Suddenly the aeroplane started to, like a rollercoaster, to drop down [with] a massive G-force. It was falling down for 20 or 30 seconds, rapidly, and then balanced, and then started once again to fall down."People then began to rush to the cockpit, he said.Israeli President Isaac Herzog said on Thursday that the alarm was raised onboard by an Israeli woman, Tali Manes, who heard a commotion coming from the cockpit. Her husband, Zvika, along with three other men - Yaniv Hayun, Dr Shota Musayev and Asaf Rajuan - entered the cockpit after Capt Machchhar managed to open the door despite his injuries. Hayun said, in a video released by the prime minister's office, that the attacker was "trying to destroy the instruments in order to disable the plane".Hayun then described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him outside the cockpit before other passengers helped to pin him down.He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane. "The plane started to level out, a bit more, and then [another] pilot told me he was taking control from there," he said.In an interview with CNN on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu said the stabbed pilot, passengers and second crew had "managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster".

schema.headline: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says

title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
description: The G7 has announced 100 million barrels of oil and diesel will be released to ease supply concerns that have caused prices to skyrocket.It includes a
body: The G7 has announced 100 million barrels of oil and diesel will be released to ease supply concerns that have caused prices to skyrocket.It includes a "substantial release" of diesel within 20 days, with discussions around "additional diesel releases as necessary", G7 leaders said in a statement.The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would begin immediately and would last for four months.Under the measures, which come after US President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports, there will not be any "export restrictions on energy and energy products" between G7 members.The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.Donald Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market. That would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.Speaking later at the White House, Trump said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".Referring to the decision by the G7 to release fuel from reserves, he added that "what Europe did was a great thing.""Europe has a lot of diesel and they're going to be making a major world contribution - and so are we," he said."And we're not going to be doing the export ban, we're going to be doing what we're supposed to do."Trump had first said he backed a diesel export ban early last week, and was still considering it on Thursday, as his administration put pressure on Europe to tap its supplies.Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.Following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the co-ordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".Macron said the co-ordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point". In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners." It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen."Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said.European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.The G7 leaders said they will also co-ordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.

schema.headline: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat

title: Women given free shorts at Oktoberfest to prevent upskirting
description: One woman made €9,000 (£7,650) from a single clip, according to BR, whose investigations found that a group of professional YouTubers from Ukraine and
body: One woman made €9,000 (£7,650) from a single clip, according to BR, whose investigations found that a group of professional YouTubers from Ukraine and several people from Bavaria were behind the videos.At least 32,000 videos of women on the Teufelsrad have been in circulation, according to Munich-based daily Süddeutsche Zeitung. Some have apparently been viewed millions of times.The operator of the Teufelsrad, Elisabeth Polaczy, told the BBC that, for the past three years, she has been handing out free cycling shorts to women and girls wearing dresses, to protect them from people filming in the crowd.This Oktoberfest she has handed out more than 100 pairs, she says: "I want to do everything I can to make people feel secure."Polaczy, who is now 80, said donating cycling shorts wasn't cheap, but it was worth it for her own peace of mind. The Teufelsrad tent is hung with signs and police posters in German and English warning against filming under people's skirts, but Polaczy says it is impossible to control everyone filming with smart phones.Some waitresses at this year's beer festival say they have also started wearing cycling shorts under their dirndls.A spokesman for the Bavarian police told the BBC that since 2025, it has run a poster campaign at the Oktoberfest, warning against upskirting.This year, police arrested a 45-year-old Swiss man for using his phone to film under a German woman's dirndl. Last year there were 10 arrests for upskirting and seven in 2024.However, Josephine Ballon, who heads German non-profit organisation Hate Aid,  which aims to support victims of digital violence, told the BBC that the current law against upskirting does not provide enough protection.Although she says there are plans for a new law, current legislation "applies only when you film under the skirt", and not when a skirt simply flies up and gets photographed. The new camera glasses are also a threat, she believes.Ballon wants anyone who has uploaded intimate pictures of women on the internet to be punished, along with the platforms that put them up.Meanwhile, the city of Munich has sought to tighten up on influencers and content creators who earn money from their social media postings and who want to film at the Oktoberfest.Munich has banned broadcasting live streams from the festival and requires anyone who wants to film there to hold a permit, which is issued by the city for a fee.Hundreds of licences have been issued this year to influencers, who make money from product placement or sponsoring.

schema.headline: Women given free shorts at Oktoberfest to prevent upskirting

title: Spoilers: Is social media ruining gig surprises?
description: Spoiler alert! Is social media ruining big gig surprises? Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Big moments from Olivia Rodrigo's tour were dissect
body: Spoiler alert! Is social media ruining big gig surprises? Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Big moments from Olivia Rodrigo's tour were dissected online shortly after her opening night BySrosh Khan and Riyah CollinsBBC NewsbeatMonths before you have a chance to see your favourite artist, chances are you already know some of the big moments they have planned.  You'll also probably know the set list, the stage design, and - if you've really been paying attention - where to stand to get the best view. When it comes to films and TV series, spoilers tend to be guarded against with warnings.But for many major gigs, there's no escaping a stream of fan videos from the shows if you're online, whether you like it or not.Last week, US pop star Olivia Rodrigo kicked off her Unraveled tour, and surprises from the show, which scores of fans have paid a lot of money to see, have already been dissected online.Tours by Harry Styles, Charli XCX and Ariana Grande have also been filmed from every angle and shared over the past few months.While some fans lap up the opportunity to see what's coming, others are taking extreme measures to preserve the element of surprise. Image source, HandoutImage caption, Aurélia Collins always aims to go to gigs not knowing what to expectAurélia Collins is one of them, spending weeks trying to trick her algorithm into not serving her content about her favourite artists and tapping "not interested" when videos come up, even though she says "it hurts my soul". It can mean her social media feed is a bit bland, but she tells BBC Newsbeat "it's worth it for the surprise".The 20-year-old criminology student is a huge One Direction fan and says she just about managed to avoid spoilers for Styles' Together, Together tour over summer. But when one slipped through the net about Niall Horan before she was able to see his show in London on Saturday - her first time seeing him live after being a fan for 16 years - she was "gutted"."When I was younger, we couldn't afford to go to events like this and hear live music and because it's such a moment, I really want to take it in," she says."I want the full experience, and that includes the element of surprise that people that go to the opening night of the tour can get."Image source, HandoutImage caption, Georgia McAdam says videos online help her plan her gig experience Not all fans think spoilers are a bad thing, though. In fact, Georgia McAdam claims she loves them."I'm the type of person that loves to be prepared," the 22-year-old says. "I love to know what the stage is looking like, what the set list consists of and where to stand."McAdam's a huge Olivia Rodrigo fan and sees online spoilers more as "teasers". She feels no amount of online videos can ever really take away from the excitement of the real thing. "Sometimes you get different surprise songs to what's online or you never know what an artist might do," she adds.'You have to not look at TikTok'Some artists have reacted by switching up their sets in small ways each night to make sure fans coming to later dates still see something unexpected. Taylor Swift had bespoke outfits and surprise songs during her mammoth Eras tour, Sabrina Carpenter performed unique positions during her song Juno and switched up her Nonsense outro, and Jay-Z has been changing up his set list on his current run.But the Guardian's deputy music editor Laura Snapes says it's not just fans who can benefit from these twists. "One way that they can make sure they're staying in the press is by having something different happen in their show every night," Snapes says. "Obviously, it'll be all over TikTok."Figures shared by TikTok with Newsbeat show posts using #CharliXCX have increased by more than 40% since the singer launched her Music, Fashion, Film tour last month. If you want to avoid spoilers, there's only one thing you can do, according to Snapes: "You have to not look at TikTok."If you want to be surprised, you have to protect yourself from absorbing any of that culture."Image source, Getty Images for AEGImage caption, Have you ever tried this one? Sabrina Carpenter had a number of special reveals for each show on her Short n' Sweet tourPhoebe Bridgers is taking things one step further to make sure fans are surprised at her shows - she's banning phones altogether.Those attending are required to lock their phones and any recording devices in a special pouch when they enter the venue to see the US singer. Anyone found breaking the rules will be escorted out. McAdam wouldn't support a ban on phones, saying recording at gigs is "part of the experience" for a lot of fans.But Collins says she's "not totally against it".What she'd prefer is to see more spoiler warnings on videos so fans have the option to be surprised if they want.But even if you know the set list, the staging and the outfits, "you're still probably going to get to see moments of humanity and stuff that's unplanned," Snapes adds. "I went to the Edinburgh Eras show where Taylor Swift was really snotty and she had to blow her nose. That's not part of the script."You're always going to be surprised."Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Spoilers: Is social media ruining gig surprises?

title: Tories pledge to build 50,000 new prison places
description: The Conservatives have promised to build 50,000 new prison places in England and Wales to stop criminals being released early, if they return to gover
body: The Conservatives have promised to build 50,000 new prison places in England and Wales to stop criminals being released early, if they return to government.The party said it would cost £2bn per year to build and run the new prisons, funded by spending cuts including to the foreign aid budget.On Thursday hundreds of prisoners were released early, under new rules introduced to prevent jails reaching capacity, with around 4,500 due to be freed by next summer.Labour blamed the previous Tory government for leaving "our criminal justice system at breaking point" and said the party's proposals were not "credible".The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham, which begins on Sunday.Prisons in England and Wales have been running close to capacity for years, with the latest government figures showing they are 98% full.Under the latest early release scheme, eligible prisoners can now be released on a community licence after serving one-third of their jail sentence.Those excluded include prisoners convicted of murder, manslaughter, a sexual or grooming-related offence, or a driving offence that led to a death.The government has also effectively scrapped one-year jail terms.The Tories said they would use extra prison capacity to reverse these measures.An early release programme introduced by the previous Conservative government saw more than 10,000 prisoners freed early between October 2023 and September 2024.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "A violent criminal doesn't become less dangerous just because the government has run out of prison cells."She added: "[Labour's] answer is to let dangerous offenders out even earlier instead of building the prison spaces we need."Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories are taking the public for fools. Across 14 years in government, they added just 500 prison places and closed 23 prisons. "Now Kemi Badenoch expects the British people to believe they'll build 50,000."Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy told BBC Breakfast the 50,000 extra places would be built within six to seven years "and the vast majority of them will be built in the first parliament".Meanwhile, the Prison Governors' Association said "long-term investment" was needed and warned a "staffing crisis" would pose challenges to delivering new prisons.If the party wins power, the Tories said they would introduce legislation early in the new Parliament to override planning and procurement barriers, allowing the process to be "fast-tracked".It said the use of private finance would help speed up delivery and control costs.There are currently around 89,000 useable prison places in England and Wales, according to the latest government figures.The Tories said their proposals would increase this figure by more than 50%, with the vast majority of new places expected within the party's first Parliament in government - up to five years - and the full increase delivered within seven years.The £2bn a year cost would be funded through savings in other areas, including cutting the aid budget by £1bn and reducing the budget of the Department for Culture Media and Sport by £1bn.The Labour government has promised to add 14,000 extra prison space by 2031.The Tories argued increasing prison places would cut crime and prevent reoffending by keeping serious criminals off the streets.Timothy said: "Prison works. It works by punishing and deterring, but most importantly by incapacitating. "Prison should keep violent and repeat offenders away from the law-abiding public."

schema.headline: Tories pledge to build 50,000 new prison places

title: Suppliers pile pressure on government over energy bills
description: The government should take immediate action to help those struggling with energy bills this winter, the suppliers' trade body has said.Energy UK said
body: The government should take immediate action to help those struggling with energy bills this winter, the suppliers' trade body has said.Energy UK said domestic gas prices, which rose on Thursday, and forecasts of steep rises in January meant inaction would lead to a longer-term, more costly and deeper crisis.Figures revealed by the BBC earlier this week showed forecasters predicting a 16% rise in domestic energy prices in the new year for 20 million households on variable tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the government was considering any measure that took the pressure off.Households in England, Scotland and Wales on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap, which puts a maximum price on each unit of gas and electricity, were hit with a 4% price increase at the start of October.That is the equivalent of about £60 per year - or £5 per month - taking an annual bill to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year.But forecasts show a far greater increase is possible for bills in January. Consultancy Cornwall Insight said its latest forecast suggested the same typical annual bill would rise to £1,999.On Thursday, the boss of supplier EDF Energy, Simone Rossi, warned that the UK was "walking into a second energy crisis" and Vyas said that action was needed before bills jumped again."Last-minute emergency interventions run the risk of being badly targeted and costing us all more," she said.Energy UK is calling for government measures including:targeted support over and above the £150 Warm Home Discount, given to people on benefits, which would eventually lead to the introduction of a discounted social tariffa debt relief scheme for the most severely affected households as part of a strategy that will also help prevent debt build-up among new tenants and homeownersremoving more levies from electricity bills and shifting them to taxation, as part of a wider move to electrificationAdam Scorer, chief executive of charity National Energy, which campaigns against fuel poverty, told BBC Breakfast he agreed with what Energy UK's analysis. "[The increase in debt is] not more people getting into debt, that's more poor people getting into more serious levels of debt." He added: "Until you do something about that, there's no way forward, there's no breathing space, there's no future for households who can't see their way beyond debt."At the Labour Party conference last week, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC that he would not call Rossi's crisis warning an overstatement, adding that the cost of home energy, as well as petrol and diesel, was "very difficult indeed"."We're looking at any measure that can give people breathing space, that can take the pressure off," he said.

schema.headline: Suppliers pile pressure on government over energy bills

title: 'G7 strikes oil deal' and Alison's TV heart scare'
description: The Sun leads on, external the terror charges brought against the man accused of killing Reform UK spokeswoman Ann Widdecombe. The paper says the poli
body: The Sun leads on, external the terror charges brought against the man accused of killing Reform UK spokeswoman Ann Widdecombe. The paper says the police are linking Joshua Kerry to an alleged firebomb attack on the party leader, Nigel Farage's home last year. "Ann suspect on Nigel terror rap" reads its headline.The Times says the price of diesel, external at the pump is expected to fall, after European leaders struck a deal with Donald Trump to release emergency stockpiles of fuel. The report says that would avert a US export ban, previously threatened by the President.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch says her party would cut foreign aid to pay for 50,000 new jail cells, according to the Daily Mail, external. The paper calls it the biggest prison-building programme since the Victorian era.The Daily Telegraph says the United Arab Emirates, external has threatened to pull billions of pounds of investment out of the UK, in retaliation for Manchester City being found to have broken Premier League financial rules. Its report says in the weeks before the verdict was announced the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, held a meeting with the club's chairman, but the Department for Business insists the two men didn't discuss football.The Financial Times says Chancellor, external John Healey's first Budget this month is expected to provide "breathing space" for households and businesses, rather than impose tax rises. The paper says big decisions have been parked until next year and that Labour insiders have said Healey's main aim is to reassure investors. One senior party figure is quoted as saying "it won't be a blow-the-doors-off budget".School inspections in England will be changed for the second time in a year according to the Guardian, external. The paper says the new system - introduced after the death of a headteacher - has received a barrage of complaints that it's damaging school leaders' mental health. Education Secretary Lucy Powell will reportedly tell the regulator, Ofsted, to "go back to the drawing board".The Daily Mirror leads on, external what it calls the TV presenter, Alison Hammond's "heart scare". The 51-year-old was rushed off air after clutching her chest during This Morning yesterday. Its front-page features a picture of Hammond in her hospital bed, who later said she was getting her "old ticker checked out".

schema.headline: 'G7 strikes oil deal' and Alison's TV heart scare'

title: Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution, lawyer says
description: Pike's lawyers filed an emergency motion on Friday to preserve "any and all evidence" related to her botched execution.Hospital staff are working to s
body: Pike's lawyers filed an emergency motion on Friday to preserve "any and all evidence" related to her botched execution.Hospital staff are working to save her life and clear the drug used, pentobarbital, from her system, the filing states.During the execution attempt, prison officials tried to start intravenous (IV) lines by using at least seven needles on Pike, according to her lawyers.At one point, Pike herself offered guidance of where they could try."One needle was bent in a 90-degree angle when it was removed," the filing states.While receiving the two doses, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said.Tennessee Governor Bill Lee ordered an independent review into Pike's botched execution and he halted all executions in the state for the year.The state's department of correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have not not offered any explanations about what went wrong.Pike's attorneys previously warned that her conditions, including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.In the latest filings, her lawyers allege that "at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike's body".They are requesting that all relevant physical, written and electronic evidence is preserved.Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, said two doses of pentobarbital was enough that "she would have surely died" had it entered her bloodstream in normal circulation.The only possible explanation for her survival, Zivot said, "is that the pentobarbital blood level was never high enough to cause death" and that blisters on her arm after the botched execution indicated a ruptured vein.So, instead of entering Pike's bloodstream, he said, the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under her skin.Pike's medical condition of thrombocytosis may have also played a role, forming blood clots at the injection site that would potentially block pentobarbital from entering her veins.Regarding the possibility the pentobarbital was degraded, Zivot explained that if this was the case, it could be due to factors including poor manufacturing or improper storage.

schema.headline: Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution, lawyer says

title: Why thousands of couples are choosing Scotland to say 'I do'
description: Chihon, from Chile, and Anna Maria, from Moldova, came to Scotland to study, but the country quickly became the backdrop to their love story.The coupl
body: Chihon, from Chile, and Anna Maria, from Moldova, came to Scotland to study, but the country quickly became the backdrop to their love story.The couple first met in 2018 through a dance society at the University of Edinburgh, when Anna Maria was on an Erasmus exchange and Chihon was completing his postgraduate studies.They they spent years as friends, and it was not until Anna Maria returned to Edinburgh in 2024 that their relationship became something more. And their romance blossomed in the same place their friendship had years earlier."Everything happened again on the dance floor," Anna Maria said.Just four months after getting engaged, the pair walked down the aisle on the Isle of Arran.The couple said they "fell in love" with the island at first sight, due to it having the "complete scenery of Scotland". "You feel that you're in a magical place", said Chihon. "It's very unique."The couple said Scotland felt like the natural choice."We're from two different continents," Chihon said. "Scotland is where we met and where we built our life together."

schema.headline: Why thousands of couples are choosing Scotland to say 'I do'

title: Two men charged with terrorism offences in Manchester
description: Two Iranian nationals who arrived in the UK by small boat have been charged with terror offences over an alleged plot to target the Jewish community i
body: Two Iranian nationals who arrived in the UK by small boat have been charged with terror offences over an alleged plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester.Rahman Salehi, 34, of Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool, are accused of preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism on or before 20 September.The men were arrested in Manchester's Northern Quarter on the eve of Yom Kippur, considered the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said news that two Iranian men had been charged over the alleged plot would be "deeply distressing" to Manchester's Jewish community, as the city marks one year since the Heaton Park Synagogue attack.Counter Terrorism Police (CTP) allege the two men were in contact with a third-party overseas, who may be in Iran, in relation to the plot.According to CTP, the men are accused of obtaining instructions to make a chlorine bomb, acquiring liquids, components and equipment for such a device, researching potential targets and conducting reconnaissance of potential locations for attack.Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the suspects had arrived via small boat in 2020 and 2023. One was granted asylum, and the other has a live asylum claim.She added: "These recent events are a stark reminder of the threats posed against this country from both terrorists and foreign state actors."Two suspects have been charged with planning a terrorist attack against Jewish communities in Manchester."This news will be deeply distressing for our Jewish communities, coming so soon after Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur."I know this will be especially true in Manchester, as we mark one year since the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue."The fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago is a reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country. While numbers are down, I know there is more we must do."It would be inappropriate to comment further on this case. But I can say that we will be unrelenting in our efforts to protect our Jewish communities, root out antisemitism in this country, and maintain our border security."

schema.headline: Two men charged with terrorism offences in Manchester

title: Rui Pinto: Hacker who released Man City documents fears for life as he prepares to lose witness protection
description: Pinto became part of Portugal's witness protection programme in 2020 after agreeing to co-operate with authorities and provide files obtained through
body: Pinto became part of Portugal's witness protection programme in 2020 after agreeing to co-operate with authorities and provide files obtained through the Football Leaks operation.He posted on X on Friday, external that the decision to terminate his participation in the programme on 10 October has put him in a "life-threatening situation".The 37-year-old said it had left him with no alternative but to relocate to an undisclosed location for an indefinite period because of "multiple death threats" and "the serious risk of an assassination attempt".BBC Sport has approached the Commission for the Protection of Victims of Crimes in Portugal for comment.Pinto has described himself as a whistleblower, but was convicted in Portugal of offences including illegal access to data and attempted extortion and given a four-year suspended sentence.He wore a bulletproof vest during his first trial in 2020, which was also subject to heightened security measures.Earlier this year, he was acquitted in a second trial of 241 counts of illegally accessing email accounts belonging to a number of sports bodies in Portugal, including Benfica.On Wednesday, Pinto turned his attention to Fifa president Gianni Infantino, saying he had "become a cancer on football" and should "have no place in the future of the game".Pinto repeated allegations from 2018 that Infantino intervened to help City and Paris St-Germain avoid financial fair play sanctions from European football's governing body Uefa.Infantino's position has recently come under increased pressure following controversial plans to sell stakes in the governing body's competitions, such as the World Cup, to private investors. A statement from Pinto's lawyers released on Friday said the decision to end his participation in the witness protection programme left him at heightened risk, noting legal proceedings stemming from the leaks remained ongoing, including the case against Manchester City.Pinto has set up a fundraising page to help him "survive this serious situation", which he claims was "created by the Portuguese State".

schema.headline: Rui Pinto: Hacker who released Man City documents fears for life as he prepares to lose witness protection

title: Man City guilty charges: Which clubs did 'inflated' money flow to in transfer market?
description: Manchester City's spending power unquestionably changed the world football transfer market - their willingness to pay higher fees and wages meant pric
body: Manchester City's spending power unquestionably changed the world football transfer market - their willingness to pay higher fees and wages meant prices rose for everybody else too.And once the world knows that a club has a wedge of cash burning a hole in its pocket courtesy of City, it can be difficult to spend it.Asking prices may rise, and having an influx of money is no guarantee of it being well spent.For many of the teams to whom City paid the most during this time, the money did not work out particularly beneficially.Let's take a look at some of the more interesting cases.First up, Wolfsburg. They immediately signed winger Julian Draxler for about half the fee received for Kevin de Bruyne in 2016, as well as others including veteran defender Dante.Having lost De Bruyne, they dropped from second to eighth in the Bundesliga before narrowly avoiding relegation in the subsequent two seasons.And things did not go particularly well for second highest-ranked club Monaco either. The most direct replacements they signed following the sales of Benjamin Mendy and Bernardo Silva in the same summer to Manchester City - Terence Kongolo and Keita Balde - did not work out in the long run, and the team went from winning Ligue 1 and reaching the Champions League semi-finals to almost being relegated within two years.The club City purchased most players from in the 2009-18 period - Arsenal (four) - did not mount a serious Premier League title challenge during that time.Some clubs who did not receive payments from City could also argue that the spending of money from their "inflated" accounts compromised their chances.For example, Manchester City paid very similar totals to Benfica and Porto during the era, but nothing to Sporting, the club which makes up the big three in Portugal.Sporting did not win a title between 2009 and 2018. There are many reasons for that, but could one of them be the fact that their direct rivals received money from City that would perhaps not have been on offer had they followed football's financial rules?Of the 12 clubs who received the highest amount of money from Man City, only the two Portuguese clubs won a major trophy within less than four years of the player sale(s).There are also some ancillary fees which reached clubs whom Manchester City did not deal with directly.Some players were subject to sell-on clauses, where the club City where buying the player from owed money to the previous team who owned the player.For example, Queens Park Rangers earned roughly £9m from Raheem Sterling's move to City from Liverpool in 2015.Barnsley took about £7m of the transfer fee paid to Everton for John Stones in 2016, and the Toffees also had to pass on about £2.5m to Wolves when Joleon Lescott moved to Manchester in 2009.The Sterling and Stones clauses were worth more than most players operating in the English Football League at that time, significantly strengthening the financial positions of QPR and Barnsley.To this day Barnsley have not sold a player for a higher amount than the fee they are believed to have received for Stones.But QPR have not returned to the Premier League and Barnsley dropped down to League One from the Championship after two seasons.Manchester City's spending during the time in which they were breaking the rules certainly had an enormous impact, on their own upward trajectory, the futures of other clubs around the world and the wider football economy.But the reality is that it is impossible to unweave the tapestry of football history during that time and since - too much has happened and there are too many indirect consequences.The effects of that spending will reverberate for years to come.

schema.headline: Man City guilty charges: Which clubs did 'inflated' money flow to in transfer market?

title: Met Police urge pro-Palestine students to move 7 October protest
description: The Metropolitan Police is calling on the organisers of a pro-Palestinian student march planned to take place on the third anniversary of the 7 Octobe
body: The Metropolitan Police is calling on the organisers of a pro-Palestinian student march planned to take place on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks on Israel to move the event.Deputy Assistant Commissioner James Harman said the force had been unable to identify the organisers behind the group, which calls itself the University of London Coalition. He said that while the march did not meet the strict legal threshold at which police could request the home secretary to ban a protest, many Londoners would be marking "a day of mourning" with vigils to remember those who died.The BBC has contacted the group for comment via social media accounts they appear to be associated with.Harman said around 300 students were expected to march through central London, from King's College London in the Strand on Wednesday, finishing at University College London in Holborn.He said they had demanded an end to what they described as a "genocide in Gaza". "Serious concerns have been expressed about the impact of this march on students and staff, particularly those who are Jewish, the route, and the day it is being held," Harman said. He urged anyone intending to join the protest to "reflect on the impact and distress it will cause on this very significant day, and exercise your right to protest on a different date".Harman said the force had written to four London universities to ask them to engage with their students and staff and to take "all reasonable steps" to ensure students did not feel "excluded, targeted or unsafe" due to activity on their premises.He said the letter acknowledged "the importance of freedom of expression, peaceful protest and academic debate" but also pointed to findings from the Community Security Trust over a rise in antisemitic incidents at UK universities since the attacks in 2023. A march can only be banned if police consider it would result in serious public disorder, and that placing restrictions on it would not prevent that disorder from taking place. The decision needs approval from the home secretary.Harman said he did not believe the strict legal threshold required in order to request such a ban had been met. Neither the police or the home secretary can ban static demonstrations, although conditions can be placed on them.Harman said that if the march went ahead, police would use their "full powers" to ensure there were "appropriate conditions" in place, including on the route and timing of the march. Police say anyone who breaches conditions will be arrested and officers will take a zero-tolerance approach to hate crime. Harman said although officers had made "every effort through formal and informal channels" to identify the organisers behind the event, they had been unable to do so. "If it goes ahead, we will have to police it," he added. Around 1,200 people were killed by Hamas fighters in the attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, and 251 people were taken hostage.This triggered a massive Israeli military offensive in Gaza, which has killed over 70,000 Palestinians. In June, a UN commission of inquiry concluded that Israel is committing genocide, and a resolution passed by the International Association of Genocide Scholars (IAGS) in September came to the same conclusion.More than 900 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza this year despite the ceasefire, according to latest figures from the territory's Hamas-run Ministry of Health. Another pro-Palestinian protest is planned for Saturday 10 October, with 10,000 people expected to attend, as well as a counter-protest, which police said will be subject to strict conditions.On Sunday 4 October, around 5,000 people are expected to attend a march in Whitechapel to mark the 90th anniversary of the Battle of Cable Street.Police said they were not expecting disorder, but officers would be present in case of "disagreement between different groups" attending the event. Harman said each of the events, along with the Holborn and St Pancras by-election for Sir Keir Starmer's seat on 8 October, represented a "challenge for policing".He said officers had arrested three men, following reports of "intimidating and obstructive conduct" during canvassing in recent weekends, and "conflict between those canvassing and protesters". Harman said that where police had intervened, it was for the purpose of preventing crime and disorder and not on any political preference, insisting "it's not a two-tier approach".The Met says it expects more than 600 officers will be involved in policing the various protests and events over the next week, coming at a financial cost but also drawing officers away from day-to-day policing in London. title: Why electric cars might be making some passengers feel sick
description: EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be whyImage source, Getty Images/Halfpoint ImagesByGrace DeanLola Baird has jus
body: EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be whyImage source, Getty Images/Halfpoint ImagesByGrace DeanLola Baird has just asked her boyfriend to pull over. Forty minutes into a journey and she's feeling "overwhelmed" by nausea - and can't stop herself throwing up on the ground next to his car.Lola, 24, from north London, had never experienced motion sickness until her boyfriend bought an electric vehicle (EV) two years ago. Ever since, she's been feeling "very nauseous" when he takes her on long car journeys.It's become so severe she's even asked him to change his car.Lola isn't alone. Other people told BBC News that they or their children notice feeling more car sick when sitting as a passenger in an electric vehicle. But at the same time, many EV drivers say it's not been a concern.So what could explain these reports of motion sickness?Dr Irene Di Giulio, senior lecturer in anatomy and biomechanics at King's College London whose research includes motion sickness, says research so far suggests some people experience more severe motion sickness in electric vehicles than in non-electric vehicles.It's something Dr Nicholas Hac, a neurologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago who specialises in dizziness and vertigo, has also heard from some of his patients. "They just notice that they're much more likely or prone to be motion sick" in electric vehicles, he says."I've heard about it many, many, many times," he adds, saying about two patients a month specifically reference feeling motion sick in electric vehicles.Image source, Lola BairdImage caption, Lola Baird noticed that she felt sick in electric vehicle taxis as well as her boyfriend's car. "I started to put two and two together," she saysBut research into any possible link is still in its early stages, and some academics say there isn't sufficient evidence to say anything definitive.Dr Bill Yates, who has researched motion sickness at the University of Pittsburgh, says the body of research is "pretty sketchy at this point"."There's some anecdotal information, but not a lot of really serious, extensive studies done yet," he says.'Wonderful to drive... but my daughter gets unwell'When Mark Quigg was looking at options for a new car last year, an electric vehicle seemed like the best choice because of the lower running costs. Mark, 45, from Lincolnshire, says his shiny new electric vehicle has been "wonderful" to drive - but he quickly noticed that his nine-year-old daughter's motion sickness got much worse in it.She only used to get motion sick on their 600-mile drives to France during the school holidays, but now he says even the 30-minute trip to the nearest city makes his daughter feel unwell.On one recent journey, he says his daughter even threw up, which had never happened before.Image source, Mark QuiggImage caption, Mark Quigg says electric cars are a "lovely driving experience for me, personally, because they are a lot quieter"Motion sickness doesn't affect all EV passengers - many owners got in touch with BBC News to say they and their relatives don't get sick in electric vehicles. Others said they felt less sick in EVs compared with traditional combustion engine cars.Vicky Edmonds, the CEO of EVA England, an association for electric vehicle drivers, says motion sickness isn't a concern among her members. "This has never come up as an issue," she says.But Chinese electric vehicle maker XPeng, which has showrooms across the UK, has previously publicly addressed the issue, external, telling people who've noticed a link between electric vehicles and travel sickness that "it's a fair question, and it's not your imagination". It's caused by "side effects of how electric cars are engineered," it adds.What could cause it?Motion sickness is caused by "a mismatch in sensory cues," Hac says. Our bodies rely on three main sensory inputs to show that we're moving, which come from what we see, what our inner ear's balance system perceives, and what fibres in our body sense, he says. When one of these is in conflict with the others - like if you're looking at your phone so you don't see visual signs of movement out of the window - that can cause motion sickness.Research suggests several reasons why it may be more severe in electric vehicles.Humans have adapted to associate sound with movement in vehicles, experts explain. Because electric vehicles don't have the auditory cues and vibrations from the engine that we're used to, which indicate when the car is accelerating, this could trigger motion sickness, Di Giulio says.Another reason is regenerative braking, the process whereby when drivers release the accelerator, the electric car starts to slow down and uses the energy to feed the battery. However, it is a process that needs to be done smoothly with the accelerator being released gently, or it can lead to harsh deceleration."It forces the person to perhaps feel like they're rocking back and forth for that brief moment when the speed of the car suddenly changes," says Hac.This is something Carolyn Le, 24, from California, has noticed. She gets "horrendous" motion sickness when her friend drives her in his electric vehicle in busy cities, she says. The regenerative braking means it "constantly feels like the car is stopping all the time".Image source, Carolyn LeImage caption, "It's actually horrendous," says Carolyn Le, who blames regenerative braking for her motion sicknessElectric vehicles can also accelerate and decelerate much more quickly than conventional combustion cars, which Di Giulio says can cause motion sickness.Edmonds, of EVA England, says developments in electric vehicle design have made them better at moderating the acceleration so they don't gain speed as rapidly.She adds that the association thinks motion sickness in an electric vehicle is caused by "other factors" like the motorist's driving style rather than the vehicle itself. Some people are also just more prone to motion sickness, and genetics have the biggest influence on this, Hac says. Women and children are more susceptible, experts say. Motion sickness typically peaks between the ages of eight and 10, after which it decreases through more exposure, says Prof John Golding, who has researched the subject at the University of Westminster, the Royal Navy and the RAF.Hold your head still and open the windowAs their popularity increases, avoiding electric vehicles can be a challenge - the number of new zero-emission cars registered in the UK rose by 40.5% in April to June 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, latest Department for Transport figures show. , externalAt the end of June 2026, 5.8% of all licensed cars on UK roads were zero-emission vehicles, the data shows. The sale of new purely petrol or diesel cars is set to be banned from 2030.Lucinda Harrison, 24, from London says she often books taxis that turn out to be electric vehicles, and has to endure the trip feeling nauseous, sweaty and clammy.The thought of travelling in an EV fills her with dread, she says. Even just a five-minute lift from a colleague to a Tube station recently was enough to make her feel "horrific".Academics say there are several steps passengers can take to reduce feelings of motion sickness.Look out of the front window and don't look at your phone or read a bookSit in the front passenger seat rather than in the back, if possible. If you do have to sit in the back, opt for the middle seat so you can still see out the front windowKeep your head still by holding it against the headrestRecline your seatRegulate your breathingOpen the window to let in fresh airTake travel sickness tablets if needed, though these can cause drowsinessBefore a long journey, make sure you're hydrated, have slept well and have eaten non-greasy foodExperts also say we can become desensitised to motion sickness through prolonged exposure. The more journeys you take in electric vehicles, the less likely you are to become motion sick as your body adjusts, Golding says.Image source, Getty Images/Cyndi MonaghanImage caption, Looking out the window can ease motion sickness, which children and women may be more prone to experiencing as passengersThere are also things carmakers can do to alleviate motion sickness in electric vehicles, says Prof Cyriel Diels, professor of mobility design at the Royal College of Art. These include having software that smooths out rapid acceleration, adding sound systems and subtle seat vibrations to signal to passengers that the car is moving, and offering adaptive regenerative braking that reduces sudden deceleration.Matt Adams from BEAMA, which represents UK manufacturers of electric vehicle charge points, says he's confident that "if future research identifies the reason for car sickness that vehicle manufacturers can respond and improve accordingly".But for Lola, she just wants her boyfriend to trade in his car. She says that day can't come soon enough.Get in touchAre you an EV driver or have been a passenger in an EV? Have you experienced nausea due to motion sickness? Tell us your story.

schema.headline: Why electric cars might be making some passengers feel sick
